paragraphs.text: Archaeologists believe that ice skating probably developed thousands of years ago, and helped people to travel more widely during the severe winters in central and northern Europe. The remains of the first known ice skate, recovered largely intact from a lake bottom in Switzerland, date back to about 3000 BC. The extensive distribution of similar evidence of skating has made it difficult for scientists to pin down exactly when and where ice skating first began. However, biomechanists Dr Federico Formenti of Oxford University in the UK, and Professor Alberto Minetti of the University of Milan in Italy believe that its birth probably took place at roughly 5000 BC in southern Finland, which has the world's highest concentration of lakes. The thousands of lakes freeze during winter, and people living amongst them have always struggled to survive the bitterly cold months. Ice skating probably began in this particular area because the long, thin lakes acted as natural barriers which early inhabitants somehow had to frequently cross and re-cross in order to accomplish vital tasks, such as hunting for food. People probably first made ice skates in order to limit the energy required for the successful achievement of these routine but crucial activities.

The earliest skates were constructed of carved, shaped horse or cow bones with holes bored in the ends, and skaters attached them to their feet with leather straps. The bone 'blades' were flat on the underside, which made it difficult if not impossible to attain significant forward momentum without an added push. The skaters had to push themselves forward with a pole. However, the surface of the animal-bone blades was oily, which reduced resistance to motion and made the skating relatively smooth.

After early man learned to work with metals, these were used instead of bone for blades. In the 1300s, the Dutch started making wooden skates with iron blades, but the blades were still flat and attached to the foot with leather straps. However, around 1500 they developed a thin, narrow double-edged iron blade and this made additional propulsion unnecessary, so skaters could now push and glide efficiently with their feet. By the early 1800s, the use of a steel blade fitted to a sturdy boot had become widely adopted. Most skates incorporate that basic design today, though it has been modified and refined.

To study the energy efficiency of these various adaptations of skate design, Dr Formenti and Professor Minetti carried out a series of controlled tests. They had reproductions made of five variations of skates, from the first bone-and-pole version to later iron and steel ones, and also tested the most up-to-date skates. They assembled a team of five tested professional skaters and observed them using the various skates at an ice rink in the Italian Alps. The skaters took some time to become accustomed to the old-style skates. Once they had mastered the necessary movement patterns, the scientists measured aspects of their skating. The five skaters' heart rates, oxygen intake, leg movements and speed were recorded while they maneuvered on the skates. The tests indicated that skating on bones was relatively slow: the test skaters only reached speeds of about 3 kph. In the trials using early metal-bladed skates the skaters attained 12 kph, and with modern skates, about 30 kph. In fact, according to speed-skating records, present-day skaters can reach speeds of up to 60 kph. With the aid of mathematical models and computer simulations, Formenti and Minetti's experiments concluded that the use of skates increases the distance people can cover, and decreases the energy needed to travel over ice. For example, the researchers estimate that the first users of bone skates would have saved about 10 percent of the energy requirements that would have been needed to travel without them.

The popularity of skating as a recreational activity in Europe dates from the mid-17th century. In fact, in 1642, one of the earliest skating clubs was formed in Edinburgh, Scotland, and in 1643 the first recorded speed-skating competition was held on the frozen marshes of eastern England. Later, in 1889, the Dutch organized the world's first world skating championships where speed skating was the main event, with four different track lengths. The growing popularity of the sport led to the creation of a world sports governing body in 1892, the International Skating Union. Another significant milestone for speed skating as a sport came in 1916, when it was officially added as an event at the Winter Olympics. Today recreational ice skating includes figure skating, which combines aspects of skating and ballet, and team sports such as ice hockey.
